Most people building community do it in the wrong order: 1) Get the land! 2) Write the vision down in a document! 3) Let whoever had the money end up owning it. 4) And all the emotional preparation? Let's get around to that later, when everyone has more time!

The better order is less cinematic: 1) Practice together! 2) Process a real conflict! 3) Get clear on your values. 4) Test membership. 5) Decide ownership and exit. 6) Only then, start thinking about land. I know, it wouldn't make much of a movie!

And the money side should go in stages too: don't try to fly straight to the economic destination! Only once the group can reliably provide for everybody, and fairly decide who gets what from the common, should it move to a common purse. And cutting back on outside money, or getting rid of it? That should come from what the group has shown it can do, rather than from deciding that "money is impure!" (which sounds weird while somebody else is quietly paying the tax bill).

A group that practices together weekly for two years may never own land. So what? It can still make a difference in how people get through divorce, illness, grief, parenting and plain old loneliness.

Here's an idea if you're remote, or stuck where you are: build the part of it you actually can. Have a weekly meal with two households. Set up a counseling exchange with one friend, in person or by video. Share tools or childcare. Transport or food prep work too. Or a sauna! And if you're hippie enough, add acro-yoga, dance improv, a mothers' circle or a cuddle puddle.

If You Can’t Move

I realize that for most people reading this there are a lot of reasons why they can't just head off and go build community on some land. Jobs, kids, pets, debt, a mortgage, a sick parent, or several of these arranged in a circle... That's fine! The most important pl/ork doesn't need land anyway.

People sometimes buy forty acres and then bring all their unprocessed baggage with them to a more scenic location. The view's better, I'll give them that! But now the conflict has goats.

The inner pl/ork can start right where you live, though. Peer counseling only needs two people and enough privacy to talk. And reparenting, somatic work, jealousy, conflict repair, etc etc? None of that has to wait for a deed either!

Find two or three people to form a practice group with (call it that, not a commune). Meet regularly, and learn to listen, switch roles, handle one disagreement and keep your commitments before you start talking about a shared future. One disagreement is enough!

Where do you find them? Are there any unprogrammed Quaker meetings or restorative-practice groups near you? Any open-hearted congregations? Maybe a mature recovery group, or a meditation group? Or someone who came back from a long retreat kinder, rather than more impressed with themselves?

Decades after the Bruderhof shaped my father, I'm publishing the film he made, and writing this.

Maybe some of you will build something useful from this. Maybe that community will teach someone else, who'll build another. Passing it on doesn't need one institution, one founder or one official version.

If you build something real, maybe we'll hear about each other. And if you teach other people to build, hearing about it matters less.
